intro:
These exercises drill the chapter's central claim: matrix performance is decided by a fixed order of decisions, and the order starts with storage layout and loop order, not with the loudest accelerator. The warm-up fixes that pipeline in your mind, the code-reading and implementation tasks make you walk memory by hand and rebuild the kernels that the order recommends, and the debugging and design tasks force you to defend a placement decision with evidence rather than enthusiasm.

Throughout, the recurring lens is ownership and contiguity. A matrix is a two-dimensional idea flattened into a one-dimensional Vec<f32> by the offset = row * cols + col rule, and every optimization in the chapter is really a question about which traversal that rule makes cheap. Get the layout and loop order honest first; SIMD, tiling, parallelism, and GPU offload only pay off once the local memory walk is already contiguous.

exerciseSolutions.title: State the optimization order and why it holds
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The pipeline runs left to right, cheapest-to-get-right first: storage layout, then loop order, then SIMD, then blocking/tiling, then CPU parallelism, and only last GPU offload. Each stage is cheaper to verify and harder to get wrong than the one after it, and each later stage silently assumes the earlier ones are already settled.

The reason a clever SIMD kernel or a thread pool cannot rescue a bad layout or loop order is that those later levers multiply throughput on top of the memory traffic the earlier stages produce; they do not reduce that traffic. If the inner loop walks a column of a row-major right-hand matrix, every step strides across a fresh cache line, and vectorizing or parallelizing that loop just spreads the same cache-miss-bound work across more lanes or cores. SIMD needs data that is already contiguous to load a full register cheaply; parallel workers still each pay the per-element miss. You cannot vectorize your way out of a layout that defeats the cache, because the bottleneck is memory bandwidth and latency, not arithmetic units.

GPU offload is reached last and least often because the kernel runtime is only one term in the end-to-end cost: you also pay device wait, host-to-device copy, launch, and device-to-host copy. For most workloads a layout-and-loop-order fix on the host removes the bottleneck entirely, so the GPU stage is entered only after the layout question has been answered and the host path is genuinely saturated.
criteria: Order stated as storage layout and loop order, then SIMD, tiling, parallelism, and GPU offload last.
Explains later stages multiply throughput over the memory traffic earlier stages produce, so layout and loop order must be honest first.
Notes GPU offload is rarely needed and only entered after the host layout question is settled.

exerciseSolutions.title: Trace the CSR frontier step
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The input frontier is [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0], so only rows 0 and 2 are active; rows 1, 3, and 4 have frontier value 0.0 and hit the `continue` before doing any work.

Row 0 reads the slice indptr[0]..indptr[1] = 0..2, which selects indices[0..2] = [1, 2]. So row 0 reaches columns 1 and 2, and the loop sets next[1] = 1 and next[2] = 1 (data at those edges is 1.0, which is nonzero). Row 2 reads indptr[2]..indptr[3] = 3..5, which selects indices[3..5] = [3, 4]. So row 2 reaches columns 3 and 4, setting next[3] = 1 and next[4] = 1. Note the slice bound for row `r` is indptr[r]..indptr[r + 1]; the starter prompt's `indptr[row]..indptr[row + 1]` is the half-open range of edge slots owned by that row.

After both active rows, the next vector is [0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Column 0 is never reached by any active row, so next[0] stays 0. Inactive rows are skipped entirely because a zero frontier value means that vertex is not part of the current breadth-first wavefront, so its outgoing edges contribute nothing this step; skipping them is exactly what makes the sparse traversal touch only active edges instead of the whole matrix.

graph.nnz() returns data.len() = 6, the number of stored nonzero edges. graph.dense_bytes() returns rows * cols * size_of::<f32>() = 5 * 5 * 4 = 100 bytes, the cost of materializing this graph as a dense matrix. The contrast is the point of CSR: the structure pays a little metadata (the indptr and indices arrays) to store only the 6 real edges and to visit only active outgoing edges, instead of allocating and scanning 100 bytes of mostly-zero dense storage.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Step-by-step trace of one CSR frontier expansion and the nnz vs dense-bytes contrast.
criteria: Row 0 expands over indptr[0]..indptr[2] reaching columns 1 and 2; row 2 over indptr[2]..indptr[4] reaching columns 3 and 4.
Resulting next frontier is 0,1,1,1,1 with rows 1, 3, 4 skipped because their frontier value is 0.0.
nnz is 6 (data length) and dense_bytes is 5*5*4 = 100, illustrating the metadata-versus-density tradeoff.

exerciseSolutions.title: Reorder the multiply loops from i-j-k to i-k-j
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The naive kernel nests i, then j, then k, accumulating a single dot product into a local `acc` before writing out[i, j] once. The arithmetic is a sum of products over k, and that sum is associative, so we are free to reorder the loops as long as every (i, j, k) product still lands in out[i, j]. Reordering to i-k-j gives up the single-write `acc` pattern in exchange for a contiguous inner walk.

The transformation has two parts. First, hoist a.get(i, k) into a local `a_ik` immediately inside the k loop, so each element of A is read once per (i, k) pair rather than once per (i, j, k) triple. Second, make the innermost loop iterate j and accumulate a_ik * b.get(k, j) into out[i, j] by reading the current value, adding, and storing. Because k is now an outer loop, each output cell receives partial contributions across successive k iterations, so out must start at zero (Matrix::zeros guarantees that) and is added to, never reset.

The payoff is the memory walk. With i-k-j the inner loop holds i and k fixed and sweeps j, so b.get(k, j) reads consecutive offsets k * b.cols + j along a single row of B in row-major storage, one element at a time with no stride. out.get(i, j) and out.set(i, j, ...) likewise sweep one contiguous row of the output. The naive i-j-k order instead strided b.get(k, j) down a column of B (offset jumps by b.cols each step), touching a new cache line per access. The result is bit-for-bit the same up to floating-point reassociation, which is why approx_eq, with its tolerance, reports the two kernels equal on the chapter's 3x3 inputs.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: i-k-j multiply: a_ik hoisted, inner loop sweeps a row of B; equal to matmul_naive under approx_eq.
criteria: Loop nest is i, k, j with j innermost, and a.get(i, k) is read once per (i, k) via the a_ik hoist.
Innermost loop indexes b.get(k, j), striding one element along a row of B rather than across rows.
matmul_ikj returns a matrix approx_eq reports equal to matmul_naive for the same operands.

exerciseSolutions.title: Build a CSR matrix from a dense grid
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The construction is a single row-major scan of the dense buffer that records only the cells that are nonzero. We keep three growing vectors: indices and data hold one entry per stored nonzero in scan order, and indptr records, after each row, the running total of nonzeros seen so far.

Start indptr with a leading 0. For each row, sweep col from 0 to cols and read dense[row * cols + col] using the same offset = row * cols + col formula the dense Matrix uses. When a cell is nonzero, push its column into indices and its value into data. After finishing the row, push the current length of data into indptr. Because indptr[row + 1] is just indptr[row] plus the number of nonzeros found in that row, the half-open slice indptr[row]..indptr[row + 1] later names exactly that row's stored edges, which is what advance_frontier consumes.

This gives the CSR invariants directly: indptr begins at 0 and ends with one entry per row plus the leading zero, so it has rows + 1 entries, and its final entry equals the total nonzero count, which is both indices.len() and data.len(). The ownership story is simple: each pushed value is moved into its vector and never aliased, and the three vectors grow independently but stay length-consistent (indices and data always equal, indptr always rows + 1). Feeding the result into advance_frontier reproduces the same reachable columns as scanning the dense grid directly, because we stored precisely the nonzero (row, col) pairs and nothing else.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Single row-major scan that builds indptr, indices, and data with the CSR invariants intact.
criteria: indptr starts with 0, has rows + 1 entries, and its final entry equals indices.len() and data.len().
indices and data hold exactly the nonzero columns and values in row-major scan order.
Feeding the result into advance_frontier reproduces the same reachable columns as scanning the dense grid.

exerciseSolutions.title: Fix a tiled multiply that overwrites partial sums
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is that the inner statement assigns the output cell instead of accumulating into it. In a tiled multiply the k dimension is split across kk tiles, and each kk tile computes only the partial dot product for the columns it covers. The correct cell value is the sum of those partials across all kk tiles. Writing out.set(i, j, a_ik * b.get(k, j)) discards everything previous kk tiles contributed, leaving only the last kk tile's share.

This is why the bug is invisible while a.cols fits in a single tile: with one kk tile, the full dot product is computed inside that single tile pass and there is nothing earlier to overwrite, so the result matches. The moment a.cols exceeds the tile size, the kk loop runs more than once, and each pass clobbers the partial sum the previous pass deposited. The output then reflects only the final kk block rather than the whole sum over k.

The fix restores read-modify-write accumulation, exactly as the chapter's matmul_tiled does: read the current value, add the new product, store it back. The output starts at zero from Matrix::zeros and is added to across every kk tile, never reset. To catch this class of regression early, compare the tiled kernel against matmul_naive with approx_eq, or compare a checksum, on inputs whose k dimension deliberately exceeds the tile size, so the multi-tile path is actually exercised. A test with k smaller than the tile would have passed and hidden the bug, which is the trap; the test must straddle the tile boundary.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Restore accumulation across kk tiles and test with a k dimension larger than the tile.
criteria: Diagnosis names that successive kk tiles overwrite earlier partial sums because set replaces rather than adds.
Corrected inner statement is out.set(i, j, out.get(i, j) + a_ik * b.get(k, j)).
Proposes comparing against matmul_naive via approx_eq or a checksum on inputs whose k dimension exceeds the tile.

exerciseSolutions.title: Decide the GPU break-even for a scoring service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The 2 ms figure is only the kernel runtime. The end-to-end cost of an offload is the sum of five terms: waiting for the device to be available (queue and admission), copying inputs host-to-device across the PCIe bus, launching the kernel, running the kernel (the measured 2 ms), and copying results device-to-host. The spike's number ignores device wait and both copies entirely, plus launch overhead, so it is an underestimate of the real path by exactly the components that tend to dominate small and medium multiplies.

The order of work follows the chapter's pipeline, settled on the host before anyone touches the GPU. First fix the storage layout (one flat row-major Vec<f32>) and the loop order (i-k-j so the inner loop walks a contiguous row of B). Then add blocking/tiling so reused tiles of A and C stay hot in cache, and only after that partition the independent output rows or tiles across CPU cores, since computing C[i, j] depends on no other cell of C. Each of these is cheaper, lower-risk, and easier to verify than an offload, and for a batch scoring hot path they frequently remove the bottleneck without leaving the host. We reach for the GPU only if the tuned, tiled, parallel host multiply is genuinely compute-bound and still too slow.

The break-even size is a service fact, not a whiteboard fact, because whether the GPU wins depends on this service's measured queueing, admission, and transfer costs, not on a theoretical FLOP ratio. The offload path can be admission-bound (the device is shared and you wait behind other work) or transfer-bound (the input and output copies cost more than the kernel saves) regardless of how fast the kernel is. A 2 ms kernel wrapped in copy and queue time can lose to a tuned host multiply outright. So the recommendation is: tune the host path in the chapter's order, instrument the candidate offload with the full five-term cost on real batch sizes and real device contention, and let the measured crossover, where end-to-end offload latency drops below the tuned host latency, define the break-even for this specific service.
criteria: End-to-end cost given as device wait plus input copy plus launch plus kernel plus result copy, not just the 2 ms kernel.
Plan fixes storage layout and loop order, then tiling and CPU parallelism, before considering offload.
Ties the break-even to measured queueing, admission, and transfer costs for this service rather than a theoretical threshold.

labSolution.explanation:
The completed inner loop performs read-modify-write accumulation: it reads the current out[i, j], adds a_ik * b.get(k, j), and stores the sum back. Because k is an outer loop, each output cell receives partial contributions across successive k iterations, so out must begin at zero (Matrix::zeros provides that) and is added to rather than reset. The inner loop holds i and k fixed and sweeps j, so b.get(k, j) reads consecutive offsets along one row of B in row-major storage, which is the contiguous walk the i-k-j order exists to produce.

With a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and b = [[5, 6], [7, 8]], the product is the standard 2x2 matmul: c[0,0] = 1*5 + 2*7 = 19.0 and c[1,1] = 3*6 + 4*8 = 50.0. The full result is [[19, 22], [43, 50]], whose four entries sum to 19 + 22 + 43 + 50 = 134.0, the printed checksum. The i-k-j accumulation reaches the same values as a plain i-j-k dot product because summation over k is associative; only the memory traversal differs.

reviewAnswers.question: In row-major storage, what does the offset = row * cols + col formula encode, and which traversal does it make contiguous?
reviewAnswers.answer: It encodes the flattening rule that lays each row down end to end in a single contiguous Vec, so element (row, col) lives at linear index row * cols + col. Advancing col by one moves the offset by exactly one, while advancing row by one jumps the offset by cols. That makes walking along a row contiguous and cache-friendly, whereas walking down a column strides by cols and touches a new cache line each step.

reviewAnswers.question: Why does reordering the multiply loops from i-j-k to i-k-j change cache behavior without changing the arithmetic or the result?
reviewAnswers.answer: The result is a sum of products over k, and summation is associative, so the same products land in the same output cells regardless of loop nesting; the computed value is unchanged up to floating-point reassociation. What changes is the memory walk: in i-j-k the inner k loop reads b.get(k, j) down a column of B, striding by b.cols and missing the cache, while in i-k-j the inner j loop reads b.get(k, j) along a contiguous row of B. Same arithmetic, far better cache locality, which is why the i-k-j order is often a cheap first win.

reviewAnswers.question: What does a CSR matrix store beyond the nonzero values, and what does that metadata buy you over a dense layout?
reviewAnswers.answer: Beyond the data array of nonzero values, CSR stores an indices array giving each nonzero's column and an indptr array of length rows + 1 marking where each row's nonzeros begin and end, so indptr[row]..indptr[row + 1] is that row's slice of edges. This metadata lets you store only the nonzeros instead of every cell, and to visit only a row's actual outgoing edges rather than scanning all columns. For sparse data it trades a small, fixed index overhead for skipping the zeros entirely in both memory and traversal, as the chapter's nnz versus dense_bytes contrast shows.

reviewAnswers.question: What does blocking or tiling improve in a matrix multiply, and what costs does it add?
reviewAnswers.answer: Tiling splits one large multiply into many smaller subproblems whose working set fits in cache, so reused tiles of A and C stay hot and cold misses on reused blocks drop; each tile is also a natural independent unit of parallel work. The costs are more indexing logic, a larger tuning surface (the tile size must be matched to cache shape), and greater sensitivity to matrix size. For tiny matrices, or services dominated by queueing or serialization, the extra complexity may not move the real wall-clock story enough to justify it.

reviewAnswers.question: What are the components of the end-to-end cost of a GPU offload, and why can a fast kernel still lose the placement decision?
reviewAnswers.answer: The end-to-end cost is the sum of waiting for the device, copying inputs host-to-device, launching the kernel, running the kernel, and copying results device-to-host; the kernel runtime is only one of those five terms. A fast kernel can still lose because the path may be admission-bound (waiting behind other work on a shared device) or transfer-bound (the input and output copies cost more than the kernel saves), independent of kernel speed. The break-even size is therefore a service fact rooted in measured queueing, admission, and transfer costs, not a whiteboard FLOP ratio, and a well-tuned host multiply often wins outright.
